card.chief_complaint: spinning sensation with turning in bed

ask.changes_what: Determines which bedside exam follows: HINTS for continuous spontaneous, Dix-Hallpike for triggered episodic, orthostatic vitals for standing-triggered, ECG/monitoring for spontaneous episodic.
ask.do_not_use_when: Do not use a reassuring timing/trigger pattern alone to exclude stroke in patients with vascular risk factors, new headache/neck pain, or any brainstem symptom; obtain the targeted examination.
ask.escalation_warning: Acute continuous dizziness with any of diplopia, dysarthria, dysphagia, limb ataxia, new deafness or inability to walk unaided is a stroke pathway until proven otherwise; up to 20% of early DWI-MRI are false negative.

evidence.citation: Herr RD, Zun L, Mathews JJ. A directed approach to the dizzy patient. Ann Emerg Med. 1989;18(6):664-672.
evidence.population: 125 ED patients with dizziness evaluated with a standardized 66-item history/exam/lab protocol
evidence.quote: The best predictors, either older age, lack of vertigo, or neurologic deficit, could identify 86% of "serious" dizziness with 42% specificity.
evidence.reference_standard: Emergency physician diagnosis modified by 1-month follow-up using predefined diagnostic criteria
evidence.target_condition: 'Serious' cause of dizziness (stroke/TIA, arrhythmia, medication, seizure, other requiring admission) - composite predictor: older age OR lack of vertigo OR neurologic deficit

ask.how: Instead of asking 'what kind of dizziness', ask: Is it there now continuously or does it come in discrete episodes? How long do episodes last (seconds, minutes, hours)? Is it brought on only by a trigger (head/position change, standing) or does it arise spontaneously? Then ask about diplopia, dysarthria, dysphagia, new hearing loss, headache or neck pain.
ask.negative_finding: A clear positional trigger with seconds-long episodes and no neurologic symptoms makes central causes unlikely, but isolated dizziness can still be a vertebrobasilar stroke.
ask.pitfalls: Symptom-quality descriptors (vertigo vs lightheadedness) are unreliable: 52% of ED patients changed their descriptor on retest after ~6 minutes, so do not triage on 'type'. Do not confuse 'worse with movement' (most vestibular causes) with 'only occurs with movement' (true trigger).
ask.positive_finding: Continuous acute vestibular syndrome demands HINTS-type eye examination for stroke; triggered brief episodes point to BPPV or orthostatic hypotension (test with Dix-Hallpike or orthostatic vitals); spontaneous episodes lasting minutes-hours suggest TIA, Meniere or arrhythmia. Any associated brainstem symptom raises stroke probability.
ask.prerequisites: Patient able to give a history; screen for red-flag neurologic symptoms before deciding on examination pathway.
ask.rationale: Clarifies if the dizziness is triggered and episodic, which guides whether to perform Dix-Hallpike or other exams.
ask.title: Timing and triggers (TiTrATE: episodic vs continuous, triggered vs spontaneous) rather than symptom quality; associated diplopia/dysarthria/dysphagia/hearing loss

examine.changes_what: Positive with typical nystagmus: diagnose posterior-canal BPPV and perform Epley; no imaging. Atypical (downbeat/persistent) nystagmus: evaluate for central positional vertigo.
examine.contraindications: Relative: cervical spine instability or severe cervical disease, recent neck surgery, vertebrobasilar insufficiency, carotid stenosis; use the side-lying test as an alternative.
examine.do_not_use_when: Do not use to evaluate continuous vertigo with spontaneous nystagmus (acute vestibular syndrome) - a positional test cannot rule out stroke there. Avoid in unstable cervical spine.
examine.escalation_warning: Positional nystagmus that is downbeat, purely vertical, non-fatiguing, without latency, or accompanied by other neurologic signs warrants MRI for central positional vertigo (posterior fossa lesion).

evidence.citation: Halker RB, Barrs DM, Wellik KE, Wingerchuk DM, Demaerschalk BM. Establishing a diagnosis of benign paroxysmal positional vertigo through the Dix-Hallpike and side-lying maneuvers: a critically appraised topic. Neurologist. 2008;14(3):201-204.
evidence.population: Single primary study comparing Dix-Hallpike and side-lying tests in patients with positional vertigo (critically appraised topic)
evidence.quote: For the Dix-Hallpike test, the estimated sensitivity was 79% [95% confidence interval (CI) 65-94], specificity was 75% (33-100)
evidence.reference_standard: Clinical diagnosis of BPPV (study methodology rated very weak by the appraisers)

evidence.citation: Lopez-Escamez JA, et al. [Diagnosis of common causes of vertigo using a structured clinical history]. Acta Otorrinolaringol Esp. 2000;51(1):25-30.
evidence.population: 100 consecutive outpatients with dizziness or imbalance, 13 with BPPV
evidence.quote: positional nystagmus (sensitivity [SE] 90%, SP 63%), and the Dix-Hallpike test (SE 82%, SP 71%).
evidence.reference_standard: Concordant diagnosis by three blinded investigators reviewing a structured history (no imaging or vestibular-lab standard)
evidence.target_condition: BPPV (all canals) among outpatients with dizziness

examine.how: Patient sits upright on the bed; turn the head 45 degrees toward the test ear, then briskly lie them back so the head hangs about 20 degrees below horizontal (over the bed end or a pillow under the shoulders). Keep eyes open and watch for 30-60 s for latency, nystagmus direction and duration; sit up and repeat on the other side.
examine.negative_finding: A negative maneuver reduces but does not exclude BPPV (single-study LR- about 0.28); if the history is typical, repeat or perform the supine roll test for horizontal-canal BPPV.
examine.pitfalls: Downbeat, purely vertical or persistent (non-fatiguing) positional nystagmus without latency suggests a central cause, not BPPV; canalith repositioning should not be done reflexively. Sensitivity falls if the patient has already been treated, closes their eyes, or the head hang is inadequate.
examine.positive_finding: After a latency of a few seconds, a burst of torsional up-beating nystagmus with vertigo lasting under 60 s that fatigues on repetition indicates posterior-canal BPPV of the tested (down) ear; the AAO-HNS guideline diagnoses BPPV on this finding alone.
examine.prerequisites: Best applied to episodic, brief, positionally triggered vertigo with no spontaneous nystagmus; explain the vertigo may be provoked. Neck must tolerate extension and rotation.
examine.rationale: Directly tests for posterior-canal BPPV, which matches the classic presentation of brief, positional vertigo.
examine.title: Dix-Hallpike maneuver (posterior-canal BPPV)

examine.changes_what: Central-pattern nystagmus: treat as posterior-circulation stroke; obtain MRI/stroke consult. Peripheral-pattern nystagmus alone does not rule out stroke; combine with HIT and skew (HINTS).
examine.do_not_use_when: Not applicable to episodic/triggered vertigo without spontaneous nystagmus (use Dix-Hallpike); a fixation-suppressed or absent nystagmus makes the HINTS battery uninterpretable.
examine.escalation_warning: Vertical, pure torsional or gaze-direction-changing nystagmus in acute vertigo should trigger the stroke pathway even if the patient looks well and CT is normal (early MRI-DWI misses ~15% of posterior strokes).

evidence.citation: Diagnostic accuracy of the physical examination in emergency department patients with acute vertigo or dizziness: a systematic review and meta-analysis for GRACE-3. Acad Emerg Med. 2023;30(5):552-578.
evidence.population: ED patients with acute vertigo or dizziness; 16 studies, 1366 patients
evidence.quote: pure torsional nystagmus are consistent with a central cause of vertigo, sensitivity 50.7% [95% CI 41.1%-60.2%, moderate] and specificity 98.5% [95% CI 91.7%-99.7%
evidence.target_condition: Central cause of acute vertigo/dizziness - central nystagmus type (bidirectional, vertical, direction-changing or pure torsional)

evidence.citation: Tarnutzer AA, Gold D, Wang Z, et al. Impact of clinician training background and stroke location on bedside diagnostic test accuracy in the acute vestibular syndrome - a meta-analysis. Ann Neurol. 2023;94(2):295-308.
evidence.location: Results, 'Diagnostic accuracy of bedside examination findings' (Ann Neurol 2023;94:295; PMC10524166); full values in supplementary Table 2
evidence.population: Pooled AVS cohorts (10 studies; direction-changing nystagmus assessed in 400 central and 376 peripheral patients)
evidence.quote: considerably lower for the other tests including the test of skew (27.0% [16.1-37.9]), direction-changing nystagmus on lateral-gaze test (37.3% [27.2-47.3])
evidence.reference_standard: Delayed MRI-DWI for peripheral cases; confirmatory neuroimaging for stroke
evidence.target_condition: Central acute vestibular syndrome - direction-changing nystagmus on lateral gaze

examine.how: With the patient looking straight ahead, observe for spontaneous nystagmus and note the direction of the fast phase; then have them follow your finger about 30 degrees to the right, left, up and down, holding each position several seconds, and record whether the fast phase reverses direction with gaze. Remove fixation if possible (penlight/ophthalmoscope cover, Frenzel lenses).
examine.negative_finding: Unidirectional horizontal(-torsional) nystagmus that obeys Alexander's law and suppresses with fixation is the expected pattern of vestibular neuritis, but a peripheral-appearing nystagmus does not exclude stroke: central nystagmus patterns are seen in only about 37-51% of central AVS.
examine.pitfalls: End-gaze physiologic nystagmus at extreme lateral gaze and drug-induced gaze-evoked nystagmus (anticonvulsants, sedatives, alcohol) are false positives; fixation can suppress peripheral nystagmus and hide it. Positional nystagmus of BPPV is triggered, transient and torsional-upbeating, not spontaneous.
examine.positive_finding: Horizontal nystagmus whose fast phase changes direction with gaze (gaze-evoked, bidirectional), predominantly vertical (up/down-beat) or pure torsional nystagmus indicates a central lesion; specificity for a central cause is about 98% in pooled ED studies and was 100% (0/25 peripheral) in Kattah's AVS cohort.
examine.prerequisites: Patient must be able to hold eccentric gaze; avoid extreme lateral gaze (physiologic end-point nystagmus). Meaningful mainly in acute vestibular syndrome with ongoing spontaneous nystagmus.
examine.rationale: Helps distinguish peripheral from central causes by identifying nystagmus patterns.
examine.title: Nystagmus: direction-changing / vertical / pure torsional (central) vs unidirectional horizontal (peripheral)

examine.changes_what: Cannot stand/walk unaided (grade 3): treat as central; stroke work-up regardless of HINTS. Walks unaided: lowers but does not remove need for HINTS; still image if other red flags.
examine.contraindications: Do not attempt to stand a hypotensive, actively vomiting or obtunded patient; use the sitting test instead.
examine.do_not_use_when: Do not stand hypotensive, vomiting or obtunded patients; interpret with caution in patients with baseline gait impairment (neuropathy, parkinsonism, prior stroke, intoxication) where inability to walk is not new.
examine.escalation_warning: New inability to stand or walk unaided with acute vertigo is a central sign until proven otherwise, even with a normal CT and a peripheral-appearing HINTS; Carmona 2023 found truncal ataxia without nystagmus in 15% of acute-vertigo patients, mostly strokes.

evidence.citation: Tarnutzer AA, Gold D, Wang Z, et al. Impact of clinician training background and stroke location on bedside diagnostic test accuracy in the acute vestibular syndrome - a meta-analysis. Ann Neurol. 2023;94(2):295-308.
evidence.population: Pooled AVS cohorts (10 study cohorts, n=800; stroke and vestibular neuritis)
evidence.quote: Severe (grade 3) gait/truncal instability had high specificity 99.2% (95% CI = 97.8-100.0) but low sensitivity 35.8% (95% CI = 5.2-66.5).
evidence.reference_standard: Delayed MRI-DWI for peripheral cases; confirmatory neuroimaging for stroke
evidence.target_condition: Central acute vestibular syndrome (stroke or other central lesion) - severe (grade 3) gait/truncal instability

evidence.citation: Tarnutzer AA, Gold D, Wang Z, et al. Impact of clinician training background and stroke location on bedside diagnostic test accuracy in the acute vestibular syndrome - a meta-analysis. Ann Neurol. 2023;94(2):295-308.
evidence.location: Results, 'Diagnostic accuracy of bedside examination findings' (Ann Neurol 2023;94:295; PMC10524166); supplementary Table 2
evidence.quote: highest for a normal hHIT (79.9% [95% CI 72.2-87.5]), grade 2 or 3 gait/truncal instability (80.8% [45.1-100.0])
evidence.reference_standard: Delayed MRI-DWI for peripheral cases; confirmatory neuroimaging for stroke
evidence.target_condition: Central acute vestibular syndrome - grade 2 or 3 gait/truncal instability

evidence.citation: Systematic review and meta-analysis of the diagnostic accuracy of a graded gait and truncal instability rating in acutely dizzy and ataxic patients. Cerebellum. 2024.
evidence.population: 18 studies, 1025 patients with acute vestibular syndrome (665 ischemic strokes, 306 acute unilateral vestibulopathy)
evidence.quote: Grade 2/3 GTI had moderate sensitivity (70.8% [95% confidence-interval (CI) = 59.3-82.3%]) and specificity (82.7 [71.6-93.8%]) for predicting a central cause
evidence.target_condition: Central cause of acute prolonged vertigo/imbalance - grade 2/3 graded gait/truncal instability (GTI)

evidence.citation: Systematic review and meta-analysis of the diagnostic accuracy of a graded gait and truncal instability rating in acutely dizzy and ataxic patients. Cerebellum. 2024.
evidence.quote: grade 3 GTI had a lower sensitivity (44.0% [34.3-53.7%] and higher specificity (99.1% [98.0-100.0%]).
evidence.target_condition: Central cause of acute prolonged vertigo/imbalance - grade 3 GTI (cannot stand/walk unaided)

evidence.citation: Kattah JC, Martinez C, Zalazar G, Batuecas A, Lemos J, Carmona S. Role of incubitus truncal ataxia, and equivalent standing grade 3 ataxia in the diagnosis of central acute vestibular syndrome. J Neurol Sci. 2022;441:120374.
evidence.population: 52 prospectively studied AVS patients (stroke and vestibular neuritis)
evidence.quote: grade 2-3 ataxia to differentiate patients with vestibular neuritis from patients with stroke resulted in a 92% sensitivity (95% CI 79-100%), a 67% specificity
evidence.target_condition: AICA/PICA-territory stroke vs vestibular neuritis - grade 2-3 truncal ataxia (including inability to sit still as substitute)

evidence.citation: Kattah JC, Talkad AV, Wang DZ, Hsieh YH, Newman-Toker DE. HINTS to diagnose stroke in the acute vestibular syndrome: three-step bedside oculomotor examination more sensitive than early MRI diffusion-weighted imaging. Stroke. 2009;40(11):3504-3510.
evidence.population: 101 consecutive high-risk AVS patients (69 ischemic strokes vs 25 peripheral) at a stroke referral center
evidence.reference_standard: MRI (or CT) for stroke; normal MRI plus clinical follow-up for peripheral
evidence.target_condition: Ischemic stroke in AVS - severe truncal ataxia (cannot sit unassisted)

examine.how: With an assistant ready, ask the patient to sit unsupported, then stand, then walk a few metres. Grade truncal/gait instability: 0 = normal; 1 = mild sway but walks unaided; 2 = walks only with support/one-sided assistance; 3 = cannot stand or walk even with support (or cannot sit without arm support). If the patient cannot get up, note whether they can sit still unassisted.
examine.negative_finding: Walking unaided does not exclude posterior-circulation stroke: grade 3 instability is present in only about 36-44% of central AVS, so a patient who can walk still needs HINTS and imaging assessment when indicated.
examine.pitfalls: Peripheral vestibular neuritis causes unsteadiness (grade 1-2) that is easily over-called, especially in the elderly, the intoxicated or those with prior neuropathy; sedatives, Wernicke encephalopathy and alcohol withdrawal also produce ataxia. Grading systems differ (Lee 2006 vs Moon 2009), which changes sensitivity.
examine.positive_finding: Grade 3 instability (cannot stand or walk unaided) in acute vertigo is almost exclusively central - pooled specificity about 99% (LR+ high), and 0/25 peripheral patients in Kattah 2009. Grade 2-3 instability is more sensitive (71-81% pooled) but less specific (83%).
examine.prerequisites: Adequate blood pressure and no orthostatic symptoms; assistant present for fall prevention. Compare with baseline mobility in elderly or frail patients.
examine.rationale: Inability to stand or walk unaided is a strong indicator of central pathology, prompting urgent stroke evaluation.
examine.title: Ability to stand and walk unaided (truncal ataxia grade; inability = central marker)

Helps distinguish peripheral from central causes by identifying nystagmus patterns.
